## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to wire ConfigMaps, Secrets, and network policy in a simple feature-flag pattern.

## Key Concepts
- ConfigMaps as feature flags; in‑pod live reload without restart
- InitContainers and Secrets for defaults and credentials
- Sidecar for TLS rotation; readiness/liveness probes
- Namespace NetworkPolicy restricting egress

## Code Example
```yaml
# minimal skeleton for Deployment + ConfigMap (simplified)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: flag-service
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: flag-service
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: flag-service
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: flag-server
        image: myorg/flag-server:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        volumeMounts:
        - name: flags
          mountPath: /flags
      initContainers:
      - name: init
        image: alpine:3.18
        command: ["/bin/sh","-c","apk add --no-cache curl jq"]
      volumes:
      - name: flags
        configMap:
          name: feature-flags
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you add a cache invalidation strategy if flags frequently change?
- How would you handle large flag sets and memory constraints?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests the candidate's ability to compose namespace-scoped config reloads using standard primitives (InitContainers, sidecars, Secrets, PVCs, and NetworkPolicies) without custom operators, focusing on reliability and reload semantics.

## Key Concepts
- InitContainer bootstraps config from central API
- Sidecar monitors config changes and signals main app
- Secrets for API tokens and credentials
- Shared volume for config sync
- PVC for logs and /logs
- Namespace NetworkPolicy restricts egress to config API

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: config-reload
  namespace: <namespace>
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    spec:
      volumes:
        - name: config
          emptyDir: {}
        - name: logs
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: logs-claim
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: your-app:latest
          volumeMounts:
            - name: config
              mountPath: /etc/app/config
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /var/log/app
        - name: reloader
          image: myorg/config-reloader:latest
          command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "while true; do sleep 300; done"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: config
              mountPath: /etc/app/config
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you validate config before applying a hot reload?
- How would you handle partial reload failures or rollback?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to reason about per-namespace security controls, init workflows, and practical use of ConfigMaps/Secrets with network isolation.

## Key Concepts
- InitContainer for prep tasks and tooling installation
- Image scanning with Trivy in-cluster
- Per-namespace heartbeat and audit via ConfigMap
- Secrets for registry credentials and policy ConfigMaps
- NetworkPolicy restricting egress to vulnerability DB

## Code Example
```yaml
# Minimal skeleton for the image-scan guard
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: image-scan-guard
  namespace: TARGET_NS
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: image-scan-guard
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: image-scan-guard
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: install-tools
        image: alpine:3.18
        command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache curl ca-certificates && mkdir -p /logs"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
      containers:
      - name: guard
        image: busybox:latest
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
        envFrom:
        - secretRef:
            name: registry-creds
        - configMapRef:
            name: scan-policy
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
      volumes:
      - name: logs
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: image-scan-logs
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you scale this to large clusters with many namespaces? 
- How would you handle false positives and performance impact during pod startup?

## Why This Is Asked

Assess practical security hardening in CKAD, plus safe rollouts and rollback.

## Key Concepts

- Pod securityContext
- Container securityContext
- runAsNonRoot and runAsUser
- readOnlyRootFilesystem
- capabilities drop
- readinessProbe

## Code Example

```yaml
# Patch excerpt (illustrative)
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 1000
      containers:
      - name: processor
        securityContext:
          runAsNonRoot: true
          runAsUser: 1000
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
          capabilities:
            drop: ["ALL"]
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 9000
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
```

## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical CKAD skills: multi-resource coordination, canary rollout, and observability.

## Key Concepts
- Deployments and Services for versioned workloads
- Ingress canary routing and traffic splits
- ConfigMaps and Secrets for feature flags and TLS
- Readiness and Liveness probes
- Resource requests/limits and RBAC basics
- Observability and rollback procedures

## Code Example
```yaml
# Deployment skeletons for stable and canary
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api-stable
spec:
  replicas: 2
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: api
        version: stable
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: gateway
          image: myrepo/api-gateway:stable
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: "100m"
              memory: "128Mi"
            limits:
              cpu: "500m"
              memory: "256Mi"
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 10
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 15
            periodSeconds: 20
```
```yaml
# Canary Deployment
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api-canary
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: api
        version: canary
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: gateway
          image: myrepo/api-gateway:canary
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: "100m"
              memory: "128Mi"
            limits:
              cpu: "600m"
              memory: "256Mi"
```
```yaml
# Shared Service
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: api-service
spec:
  selector:

```
```yaml
# Ingress with canary rule (nginx-ingress)

metadata:
  name: api-ingress

    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary: "true"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary-by-header: "Canary"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary-weight: "20"
spec:
  rules:
  - host: api.example.local
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: api-service
            port:
              number: 80
```

```yaml
  name: api-tls
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Static-site serving in a per-namespace context tests PVC/ConfigMap/Secret integration, nginx config via ConfigMap, and safe multi-tenant limits with quotas and limits.

## Key Concepts

- Deployments, replicas, and rolling updates
- PVCs for shared data, ConfigMaps for content and nginx.conf, Secrets for credentials
- nginx basic auth integration via config map
- ClusterIP Service exposure and Readiness/Liveness probes
- Namespace ResourceQuota and LimitRange for multi-tenant safety

## Code Example

```yaml
# Minimal skeleton showing core resources
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: site-content
data:
  index.html: |-
    <html>...</html>
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: nginx-config
data:
  nginx.conf: |
    server { listen 80; location / { auth_basic "Restricted"; auth_basic_user_file /etc/nginx/.htpasswd; root /usr/share/nginx/html; } }
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: basic-auth
type: Opaque
data:
  # base64(encoded username:password)
  htpasswd: <base64>
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: static-site
spec:
  replicas: 2
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:stable
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
        volumeMounts:
        - name: site
          mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html
        - name: config
          mountPath: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
          subPath: nginx.conf
        - name: auth
          mountPath: /etc/nginx/.htpasswd
          subPath: htpasswd
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
      volumes:
      - name: site
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: static-site-pvc
      - name: config
```

## Why This Is Asked
Auditors assess knowledge of Kubernetes pod security hardening and defense-in-depth strategies.

## Key Concepts
- Pod securityContext vs container securityContext

## Code Example
```yaml
# Security hardening patch for collector Deployment
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: collector
spec:
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        seccomp.security.alpha.kubernetes.io/pod: runtime/default
    spec:
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 1000
        fsGroup: 2000
      containers:
      - name: collector
        securityContext:
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
          capabilities:
            drop:
            - ALL
          volumeMounts:
          - name: input
            mountPath: /data/input
          - name: output
            mountPath: /data/output
        # Preserve existing probes and resources
        # livenessProbe, readinessProbe, resources remain unchanged
```

- Document security context changes in version control

## Why This Is Asked
This question assesses the ability to design a namespace-scoped canary workflow using standard CKAD primitives: CronJob, ConfigMaps, and Deployment rolling updates. It also tests observability knowledge via PVC-backed logs, status tracking patterns, and security awareness through NetworkPolicy and InitContainer usage.

## Key Concepts
- **ConfigMaps**: canary-config holds dynamic parameters (targetImage, canaryPercent); canary-status records rollout history and last-promotion timestamps
- **CronJob**: Provides periodic reconciliation that checks configuration and triggers conditional updates
- **Deployment RollingUpdate**: maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 ensures controlled, non-disruptive updates
- **Traffic Shifting**: Routes a configurable percentage of traffic to canary pods for gradual exposure
- **InitContainer**: Ensures jq availability for JSON parsing within the job
- **Probes**: Readiness gates ensure traffic only reaches healthy pods; liveness checks restart unhealthy instances
- **NetworkPolicy**: Restricts namespace egress to approved registries only
- **PVC**: Persists job logs for debugging and audit trails

## Trade-offs
- **Pros**: Fully Kubernetes-native with no external dependencies; ConfigMap history provides auditability; automatic promotion reduces manual intervention
- **Cons**: Namespace-scoped only; NetworkPolicy requires CNI support; jq dependency increases image size; ConfigMaps lack built-in validation

## Why This Is Asked
This question evaluates practical CKAD skills including per-namespace configuration management, InitContainer usage, sidecar patterns, secure secret handling, and network policy implementation.

## Key Concepts
- Per-namespace deployments with shared persistent volumes
- InitContainer for runtime dependency installation
- Inotify-based file change detection and yamllint validation
- In-service reload capabilities (nginx -s reload)
- ConfigMap and Secret integration patterns
- TLS sidecar implementation for secure communications
- Namespace-level NetworkPolicy for egress restrictions

## Code Example
```yaml
# Minimal skeleton of the Deployment
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: config-watcher
  namespace: target-namespace
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: config-watcher
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: config-watcher
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: install-tools
        image: alpine:latest
        command: ['sh', '-c', 'apk add --no-cache inotify-tools yamllint']
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:alpine
        volumeMounts:
        - name: config-pvc
          mountPath: /config/dynamic
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 30
      - name: config-watcher
        image: alpine:latest
        command: ['sh', '-c', 'while inotifywait -e modify /config/dynamic/*.yaml; do yamllint /config/dynamic/*.yaml && nginx -s reload; done']
        volumeMounts:
        - name: config-pvc
          mountPath: /config/dynamic
        env:
        - name: STATUS_URL
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: status-secret
              key: url
      - name: tls-sidecar
        image: envoyproxy/envoy:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8443
      volumes:
      - name: config-pvc
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: config-pvc
      - name: nginx-defaults
        configMap:
          name: nginx-defaults
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: config-pvc
  namespace: target-namespace
spec:
  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: nginx-defaults
  namespace: target-namespace
data:
  nginx.conf: |
    # Default Nginx configuration
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: status-secret
  namespace: target-namespace
type: Opaque
data:
  url: aHR0cDovL3N0YXR1cy5sb2NhbC9hcGkvdjEvcmVsb2Fk
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: config-watcher-netpol
  namespace: target-namespace
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: config-watcher
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          name: internal-services
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
```

## Trade-offs
- **Inotify vs polling**: Inotify is more efficient but requires file system support
- **Sidecar overhead**: TLS sidecar adds complexity and resource usage
- **Single namespace scope**: Limited to namespace-level isolation vs cluster-wide
- **PVC dependency**: Requires storage management and backup strategies
- **Container sharing**: Process communication within pod vs separate services

## Why This Is Asked
CKAD requires practical mastery of node-scoped components, DaemonSets, hostPath volumes, and real-world log shipping patterns.

## Key Concepts
- DaemonSet on each node with hostPath volumes
- Log tailing with tail -F and sidecar shipping
- ConfigMap-driven batching (BATCH_SIZE)
- NodeSelector to target workers
- Readiness/Liveness probes and lifecycle (preStop)
- Resource requests/limits and rollback strategy

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: log-collector
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: log-collector
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: log-collector
    spec:
      nodeSelector:
        kubernetes.io/os: linux
      containers:
      - name: collector
        image: busybox:stable
        command: ["sh","-c","tail -F /var/log/app.log | /usr/local/bin/shipper --endpoint http://log-portal:5000/api/v1/logs --batch-size $(BUS_BATCH)" ]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /var/log
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "100m"
            memory: "128Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "256Mi"
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 15
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /ready
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 30
          periodSeconds: 30
        lifecycle:
          preStop:
            exec:
              command: ["sh","-c","sleep 10"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /var/log
      volumes:
      - name: logs
        hostPath:
          path: /var/log
          type: Directory
``` 

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test under burst log loads and verify end-to-end delivery? 
- How would you rollback a DaemonSet rollout if a regression is found?
